text:
I have seen them so sad that I can hardly think

how, being so sad, they can never weep!...


And they are always so: whether afternoon

kisses them with kisses of soft flushes,

or clear night looks at them with its suns,

or joyful foliage shelters them with its shade...


Whether climbing the slope that leads to the hamlet,

among glaucous rows of coffee trees in bloom...

or watching the waters of some murmuring

little stream running beneath a shadowy forest...


What can those eyes have, always dreaming

and always open?...

Always moist and vague and shadowy and uncertain,

as though they were always silently imploring!


Once, on the path of a flowering grotto,

I saw a solitary ox gazing at the ground

with long insistence, as though in its longings

it were anxiously seeking its lost freedom...


And again beneath a tree and beside the cart

loaded with bundles, and later in the depths

of a clear ravine, and on the immense plain,

and in a purple-and-violet sunset...


Always sad and vague, the eyes of those kings

who are now slaves! I cannot think

how, being so sad, they can never weep—

the eyes of oxen...

translation.title: The Eyes of Oxen
translation.editorial_note: The translation retains the oxen as fallen kings and preserves the poem’s repeated question about eyes that are sorrowful yet cannot weep.
